source.title: Inverse Scaling: When Bigger Isn't Better
source.authors: Ian R. McKenzie; Alexander Lyzhov; Michael Pieler; Alicia Parrish; Aaron Mueller; Ameya Prabhu; Euan McLean; Aaron Kirtland; Alexis Ross; Alisa Liu; Andrew Gritsevskiy; Daniel Wurgaft; Derik Kauff-man; Gabriel Recchia; Jiacheng Liu; Joe Cavanagh; Max Weiss; Sicong Huang; The Floating Droid; Tom Tseng; Tomasz Korbak; Xudong Shen; Yuhui Zhang; Zhengping Zhou; Najoung Kim; Sam Bowman; Ethan Perez

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream task performance across model scale and reports inverse, U-shaped, and inverted-U trends. It argues that scaling trends can reverse and be difficult to predict, but does not measure pretraining loss scaling or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The study tests constructed downstream tasks, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss. Its plots and text report task performance against training FLOPs, so these results bear on V6 and on the curve-reversal part of V7. They do not test power-law fits, extrapolation from small pretraining runs, allocation of parameters and tokens, or architecture sensitivity. Numerical task accuracies are presented in figures, not transcribed in the text; rows therefore record qualitative text descriptions and use figure_only values. The paper also reviews findings from other studies; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports zero-shot, few-shot and through-training downstream task performance against training FLOPs for about ten model series. Its results argue that downstream performance does not always improve predictably with scale (V6). The tasks were selected through a contest to show inverse scaling, so they are adversarial cases, not a representative sample. The study does not measure pretraining loss scaling, fits, allocation or architecture.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that scaling sometimes lowers task performance consistently and sometimes produces hard-to-predict fluctuations, including U-shaped and inverted-U trends. They say understanding when and why reversals occur is needed to predict larger models' behaviour. They contrast this with scaling laws' predictable loss improvements, which they do not dispute.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates zero-shot and few-shot downstream task performance across model series and training checkpoints; does not fit power laws to held-out pretraining loss or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported task trends vary by task, model series, training stage, and number of few-shot examples. The paper notes that fine-tuning series can show stronger inverse scaling on some tasks.
record.problems: The study's tasks were intentionally selected as inverse-scaling examples, so they do not establish how representative the findings are of downstream tasks generally. Numerical results for task performance are largely shown in plots rather than given as exact values in the text. GPT-4 model sizes and FLOP counts are unknown, and GPT-4 results are available for only some tasks. The authors note limitations in individual task formulations, including label imbalance for Modus Tollens, underspecification for Pattern Match Suppression, and a possible completion ambiguity for Memo Trap.
record.rows_left_out: No task-level model-series rows were omitted. The paper also reports per-task few-shot and through-training plots and discusses results from other papers; those details are summarized only where the text gives cross-task findings in r12–r13, and cited studies are excluded because they are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss measured or fitted against parameters, tokens or compute.
No depth/width or shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Text-only language models; no other modalities or repeated-data regimes.
Performance as a function of pretraining loss is not measured. The tasks are adversarially selected, so representative downstream tasks are untested.
No exponent fitting, parameter counting, schedule, fitting-method or compute-optimal split comparisons. Downstream trend reversals are not loss-curve bending.

missing.what: Average zero-shot accuracy across 10 prize tasks versus FLOPs for all series (aggregate inverse trend)
GPT-4/GPT-4 RLHF improve on Modus Tollens, Into the Unknown and Repetitive Algebra, but do poorly on Memo Trap (possible U-shaped reversal at higher scale)

record.verdict_notes: The study accepts that loss falls predictably with scale (abstract, intro); it challenges only the step from loss to downstream tasks. The reader's V7 links were reassigned to V6, because V7 concerns fitted loss-law dependence. Selection bias matters: tasks won prizes for showing inverse scaling, so the V6 challenge applies to such tasks, not to downstream tasks in general. PaLM results come from Wei et al. (2022a). GPT-4 has no FLOP count.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities and training regimes.
The study tests performance on selected constructed tasks as model scale changes; it does not test downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or broadly representative downstream tasks.

The study reports curve reversals and variation with task, model series, few-shot examples, and training stage. It does not fit scaling exponents, compare fitting methods, test parameter-counting choices, or evaluate compute-optimal splits.
